criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and neighbourhood access to drinking water and sanitation (sewerage) services across the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Region (BAMR).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines institutional fragmentation, utility privatisation/concessions, and water regulation in Buenos Aires. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly analyses formal legal, contractual, and regulatory rules governing service access: (1) utility ownership and concession rules (single-provider and single-technology clauses requiring private wells to be blocked under AASA vs. provincial decree 878/2003 recognizing independent micro-networks); (2) tariff and expansion cost-recovery rules (shifting from full-cost infrastructure charges on newly connected users to the cross-subsidized SUMA universal service tax and CIS charge, property-value vs. metered tariffs, and ETOSS/ABSA social pricing eligibility criteria); (3) legal-tenure/urbanisation eligibility rules restricting connections to legally urbanised zones and excluding shanty towns, later modified via participatory accommodation models (MPG and Agua + Trabajo); and (4) regulatory enforcement and discretion (ETOSS strict monopoly enforcement vs. ORAB and ABSA laisser-faire tolerance of illegal neighbourhood connections and alternative suppliers).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative socio-legal and institutional comparative case study carried out circa 2004-2005, combining field research data compiled by the authors across five BAMR operators (Tables 1, 2, and 5), key-informant interviews conducted in August and September 2004, and documentary/contractual and tariff records (Tables 3 and 4). Per protocol rules, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for inclusion even without quantitative effect sizes for meta-analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete access, connection, exclusion, and affordability outcomes: operator-level water and sanitation coverage/population served in 2005 (Table 1), bi-monthly bills and connection charges before and after the 1997 SUMA tariff renegotiation (Table 3: new users' average bi-monthly cost dropping from 60.69 to 15.92 pesos), exclusion of roughly half a million shanty-town residents under legal-urbanisation clauses, and connection of 520,000 inhabitants of deprived neighbourhoods under the MPG and Agua + Trabajo programmes.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and multi-level units of analysis (five water and sanitation operators and urban/peri-urban neighbourhoods and households in the BAMR covering Capital Federal and 37 municipalities), exposure (concession agreements, regulatory regimes ETOSS vs. ORAB, cost-recovery/tariff rules, and tenure/eligibility vs. participatory accommodation rules), outcome (network coverage, new connections in deprived areas, connection affordability, and informal-settlement exclusion), and study design (qualitative comparative case study) are all clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: sanitation services in the urban region of Buenos Aires (circa 2005, when this study was carried out), a region which underwent major reforms to its public utilities during the 1990s.

The AASA concession agreement provided that new users should be connected to water and sanitation services wherever ‘‘urban realities make this possible” (which actually meant ‘‘legally urbanised zones”). In practice, this meant that the shanty towns were excluded (Botton, 2007, p. 184).
There are two water regulators in the BAMR: the Ente Tripartito de Obras y Servicios Sanitarios (ETOSS) and the Organismo Regulador del Agua Bonaerense (ORAB).

In an interview in September 2004, the President of ABSA admitted that when they discover an illegal connection which diverts water to an entire neighbourhood, the company frequently adopts a ‘‘laisser-faire” approach.

This programme contributed to improving both economic and technical access to water services as it tailored rates for poorer users and connected 520,000 inhabitants of deprived neighbourhoods to the service.

raw_response.exposure: Utility concession and ownership models (AASA, AGBA, ABSA, Sudamericana de Aguas, Marcos Paz municipal service), regulatory frameworks and enforcement discretion (ETOSS strict single-provider monopoly vs. ORAB tolerance and provincial decree 878/2003), tariff and expansion cost-recovery rules (full-cost infrastructure charges vs. SUMA universal service cross-subsidy tax, CIS charge, property-based vs. metered rates, and social pricing criteria), and legal-urbanisation eligibility rules vs. participatory accommodation schemes (MPG, Agua + Trabajo).
raw_response.outcome: Household and neighbourhood water and sanitation network coverage/connections, bi-monthly connection and service costs (affordability), exclusion of informal settlements (shanty towns), and access via alternative/independent micro-networks or wells.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Five official water and sanitation operators (AASA, AGBA, ABSA, Sudamericana de Aguas, and the Marcos Paz municipal service) and urban/peri-urban residents, neighbourhoods, and informal settlements across the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Region (Capital Federal and 37 municipalities, ~14+ million residents across operator territories circa 2005).
raw_response.rationale: This full-text empirical comparative case study meets all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). It examines water and sanitation service access across the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Region circa 2005 and directly investigates rule-type legal, contractual, and regulatory mechanisms governing access under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2 — including concession monopoly and well-closure clauses, legal-urbanisation eligibility restrictions that excluded shanty towns, expansion cost-recovery and tariff rules (the shift from user-pays infrastructure charges to the SUMA universal service cross-subsidy tax and social tariffs), and regulatory discretion/enforcement differences between ETOSS and ORAB (including provincial decree 878/2003 and de facto tolerance of illegal neighbourhood connections). It draws on primary field research data compiled by the authors in 2004-2005 (key-informant interviews and operator-level data) alongside contractual and administrative records, and reports concrete coverage, connection, exclusion, and affordability outcomes.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative comparative institutional and socio-legal case study (field research, key-informant interviews, and contractual/regulatory and operator data analysis)
